newsitem.title: BELGIUM: OLOs ogle U.S. inflation signs, ignore Bonn EMU row.
newsitem.headline: OLOs ogle U.S. inflation signs, ignore Bonn EMU row.

text.p: The benchmark spread of 10-year Belgian government bonds (OLOs) over similar Bunds held steady at what dealers said was at the low end of the recent range with OLOs benefitting from discord in Germany's ruling coalition.

The spread was at six basis points on Tuesday, steady from Monday's late level, as various European markets posted modest gains on the back of losses by the mark due to the wrangling in Bonn over the interpretation of the Maastricht criteria.
Traders said the spread gains would fade once markets realised the conflict was a mere storm in a teacup and Germany would take part in EMU regardless of the shape of its finances.

"Six basis points is on the low side...it is not just us who are gaining, it is also France and Italy," a trader said. He doubted current levels could be held. "We will go back to the middle of the 6/7 to 13/14 basis point range."
He said OLOs were well-supported, holding up as the closely watched Bunds came under pressure.
One analyst said OLOs could outperform Bunds slightly as Bunds backed up before the auction of a 30-year bond. "But with a spread of six OLOs are very expensive versus Bunds," he said.
Trading incentives could also come from U.S. data, where the market is looking for signs of growth coupled with inflation.

One trader said the market expected no surprises from this afternoon's U.S. June NAPM index, forecast at 56.4, down from 57.1 in May. However, if May leading indicators and April construction spending came out stronger than expected, there

He said the market was counting on relatively positive U.S. jobs data on Thursday. A rise in new jobs by some 100,000 was discounted as was a fall in the jobless rate, possibly to as low as 4.5 percent. Only extreme swings away from the forecasts would spark major market reactions. "The market is looking for relief from the employment report."
Analysts said that although U.S. data had begun to indicate a pick-up in growth in the third quarter, bond holders would not be worried as long as there were no signs of inflation.
Similarly, the policy-making FOMC would hold U.S. rates steady while there were no obvious pressures on wages or prices.
Accordingly, they said, it was unlikely that today's and tomorrow's FOMC meeting would already change rates. The FOMC results are due late on Wednesday.
